chunks: Muhammad ibn Musa ibn al-Mutawakkil (may Allah be pleased with him) said: 'Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Sa'dabadi narrated from Ahmad ibn Abu 'Abd Allah al-Barqi, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Abu 'Umayr, from Hamzah ibn Humran, from Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) who said:

Whoever intends to do a good deed but does not do it, one good deed is recorded for him; if he does it, ten good deeds are recorded for him. Allah multiplies (the reward) for whom He wills up to seven hundred times. And whoever intends to do a bad deed but does not do it, no bad deed is recorded against him until he does it. If he does not do it, one good deed is recorded for him because he refrained from doing it. And if he does it, it remains pending for nine hours; if he repents and regrets it, it is not recorded against him; but if he does not repent nor regret it, one bad deed is recorded against him.

key_terms.تِسْعَ سَاعَاتٍ: Nine hours (period of grace for recording a sin)
key_terms.هَمَّ: Intended or resolved in the heart

ai.seo_question: How are good and bad deeds recorded in Shia theology based on intention and repentance?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *al-Tawhid* elucidates the divine mechanism of *al-‘Amal bi-l-Qasd*, where intention serves as the precursor to action, granting a full good deed for mere sincere intent. It highlights the unique Shia emphasis on the 'nine-hour' grace period for minor sins, allowing time for repentance before the sin is fully recorded, thereby underscoring God’s mercy in the accounting of deeds. This concept reinforces the theological principle that God multiplies rewards according to His will, extending up to seven hundredfold.
